title: Pipelines: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI
scopeHtml:
Scope: pipeline anatomy and ordering, GitHub Actions concepts, mapping to Jenkins and GitLab CI, caching and parallelism, secrets and OIDC.

Scope: reusable templates, runners, artifact registries, monorepo pipelines, Android CI, pipeline health.

notes.title: Anatomy of a pipeline
notes.html:
A pipeline is a recipe of automated stages that turns a commit into a running release. Typical order: checkout → restore cache → build → unit test → lint/static analysis → security scan → package (artifact/image) → publish → deploy → smoke test. Cheap, fast checks run first (fail fast); slow ones (integration, end-to-end) run later or in parallel.

Key vocabulary: trigger (what starts it: push, PR, schedule, manual), job (a unit of work on one machine), stage/step, runner/agent (the machine), artifact (build output kept for later jobs), cache (reused downloads like node_modules), secret (hidden variable).

Worked example. Budget: developers will wait about 10 minutes before they start context switching. A 40-minute pipeline means PRs sit idle, people stack branches, and the team stops trusting it. Parallelising 4 test shards turns 24 min of tests into ~7.

Industry examples. Google's TAP runs only the tests affected by a change; Meta and Uber use the same "test impact analysis" idea.

Everyday analogy. An airport: quick ID check at the door, then bag scan, then security, then boarding gate: you never wait in the long queue before the quick check has failed you.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the slowest stage first.
  • Treating the pipeline as a script rather than code: no versioning, no review, no reuse.

notes.title: GitHub Actions in practice
notes.html:
GitHub Actions pipelines are YAML files in .github/workflows/. Concepts: a workflow has triggers (on) and jobs; each job runs on a runner (runs-on) and has steps; steps use actions (uses:) or shell commands (run:). Jobs run in parallel unless linked with needs:.

name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:                       # cancel older runs of the same PR
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read                   # least privilege for GITHUB_TOKEN

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]             # run the job once per value, in parallel
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm               # caches ~/.npm keyed on the lockfile
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  image:
    needs: test                    # only after tests pass
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

Industry examples. Most open-source projects (React, VS Code, Kubernetes parts) use Actions; reusable workflows let a platform team publish one standard pipeline for hundreds of repos.

Everyday analogy. A recipe card pinned in the kitchen: the same steps run for every order, and anyone can read it.

Common interview traps.

  • Using @main or @v4 tags for third-party actions without pinning to a commit SHA: a compromised action runs in your pipeline.
  • Forgetting needs:, so deploy starts while tests are still running.
  • Leaving default GITHUB_TOKEN with write permission everywhere.

notes.title: Same ideas in Jenkins and GitLab CI
notes.html:
The concepts map one-to-one; only the syntax and hosting differ.

Concept GitHub Actions GitLab CI Jenkins
Config file .github/workflows/*.yml .gitlab-ci.yml Jenkinsfile (Groovy)
Machine runner runner agent/node
Unit of work job / step job in a stage stage / step
Reuse reusable workflow, composite action include:, templates shared library
Hosting SaaS or self-hosted runners SaaS or self-managed you host and patch it 
// Jenkinsfile (declarative)
pipeline {
  agent any
  stages {
    stage('Build') { steps { sh './gradlew build' } }
    stage('Test')  { steps { sh './gradlew test' } }
    stage('Deploy'){ when { branch 'main' } steps { sh './deploy.sh' } }
  }
}

Industry examples. Jenkins is still everywhere in older enterprises and banks (huge plugin ecosystem, but plugin upgrades and server care are real work). GitLab CI is common where the whole lifecycle is on GitLab. Newer shops pick GitHub Actions, CircleCI or Buildkite (Uber, Shopify use Buildkite with their own agents).

Everyday analogy. Different brands of washing machine: same cycles (wash, rinse, spin), different knobs.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing Jenkins "is CI". It is one tool; it must be maintained like any server (backups, plugin updates, security patches).
  • Hardcoding credentials in the Jenkinsfile.

notes.title: Speed: caching, parallelism, artifacts
notes.html:
Three levers shorten a pipeline.

  • Caching: save dependency downloads (Maven .m2, Gradle caches, node_modules, pip) keyed by a hash of the lockfile. Cache hit means no download; cache key changes when dependencies change.
  • Parallelism: run independent jobs side by side; shard a big test suite across N runners; use a matrix for several OS/language versions.
  • Artifacts: pass the build output from the build job to later jobs instead of rebuilding. Also keep test reports, coverage and the APK/JAR/image.

Docker layer caching is the fourth: order the Dockerfile so rarely changing layers (OS, dependencies) come before code (see the Docker notes).

Worked example. A Gradle build with no cache downloads 400 MB per run (about 90 s). With a cache keyed on *.gradle* and gradle-wrapper.properties the same step takes 8 s; across 300 runs a day that saves ~7 hours of runner time.

Industry examples. Bazel and Gradle remote build caches (used at Google, Uber, LinkedIn) share compiled outputs between all developers and CI.

Everyday analogy. Meal prep: chop vegetables on Sunday (cache), cook several dishes on different burners at once (parallelism), and pass the finished dish to the next cook (artifact).

Common interview traps.

  • Cache keys that never change (stale dependencies) or change every run (never hits).
  • Caching secrets or build outputs that contain them.

notes.title: Secrets and pipeline security
notes.html:
A pipeline can reach production, so it is a prime attack target. Rules:

  • Never commit secrets. Store them in the platform's encrypted secrets (GitHub Secrets, GitLab variables, Jenkins credentials) or a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager).
  • Prefer short-lived credentials via OIDC: the pipeline proves its identity to the cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) with a signed token and gets a temporary role. No long-lived access key is stored anywhere.
  • Least privilege: the GITHUB_TOKEN and cloud roles get only what the job needs. A PR from a fork must not receive secrets.
  • Pin third-party actions/images to a digest or commit SHA; scan dependencies.
  • Protect production deploy jobs with environments that require approval.

Worked example. A leaked long-lived AWS key with admin rights in a CI variable is read by a malicious dependency's install script and used to start crypto-mining instances (a classic incident). With OIDC, the credentials expire in 1 hour and are scoped to deploy one service.

Industry examples. The 2021 Codecov and 2023 CircleCI breaches both exposed CI secrets, pushing the industry to rotate secrets and adopt OIDC and SLSA supply-chain levels.

Everyday analogy. A hotel key card that stops working at checkout, instead of a physical key you must hope nobody copied.

Common interview traps.

  • echo $SECRET in logs: platforms mask exact matches only; a base64 of it is not masked.
  • Running untrusted PR code (pull_request_target) with secrets.

notes.title: Pipeline as code and reusable templates
notes.html:
Define the pipeline in the repository (Jenkinsfile, .gitlab-ci.yml, workflow YAML) so it is versioned, reviewed and reproducible, not clicked together in a UI. For many repos, avoid copy-paste: publish a reusable workflow (GitHub), include: template (GitLab) or shared library (Jenkins) owned by a platform team. Teams call it with a few inputs.

# a team's whole workflow file
name: ci
on: [pull_request, push]
jobs:
  build:
    uses: acme/platform/.github/workflows/java-service.yml@v3   # pinned version
    with: { java-version: "21", service-name: orders }
    secrets: inherit

Version the template (@v3) so a platform change does not break everyone at once, and roll out upgrades gradually.

Industry examples. Large organisations ship "golden pipelines" so security scans and deploy steps are identical across hundreds of services.

Everyday analogy. A franchise operations manual: every branch follows the same recipe, with local variations in a short form.

Common interview traps.

  • Pipelines configured in the Jenkins UI only: no history, no review, lost if the server dies.
  • Unversioned shared templates that break all repos with one commit.

notes.title: Runners and agents: hosted vs self-hosted
notes.html:
A runner/agent is the machine that executes jobs. Hosted runners (GitHub-hosted, GitLab SaaS) are clean ephemeral VMs, zero maintenance, billed per minute. Self-hosted runners give access to private networks, GPUs or special hardware, larger machines, and lower cost at scale, but you must secure and patch them.

Hardening: run each job in a fresh, ephemeral environment (container or VM destroyed after the job) so one job cannot poison the next; never run untrusted fork code on persistent self-hosted runners; autoscale (Kubernetes-based runners, Actions Runner Controller, Karpenter) so builds do not queue at peak.

Worked example. At 9 a.m. 80 PRs open at once; 10 fixed runners queue jobs for 25 minutes. Autoscaling to 60 ephemeral runners drops the wait to under 2 minutes, and idle capacity scales to zero at night.

Industry examples. Buildkite (used by Shopify, Uber) runs agents in your own infrastructure; many firms run Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes.

Everyday analogy. Renting a taxi per ride (hosted) versus owning a fleet (self-hosted): cheaper per ride at scale, but you maintain the cars.

Common interview traps.

  • Persistent self-hosted runners that keep files and credentials between jobs.
  • Optimising build time when runner queueing is the real delay.

notes.title: Artifacts and package registries
notes.html:
Pipelines produce artifacts: JAR/AAR, npm packages, Docker images, test reports, APKs. Store releases in an artifact repository (Nexus, Artifactory, GitHub Packages, ECR, Maven Central) rather than rebuilding later. Principles: artifacts are immutable and traceable (commit SHA, build number, SBOM); release and snapshot repositories are separate; old artifacts follow a retention policy.

Use an internal proxy/mirror of public registries: builds keep working when npm or Maven Central is down, and you can block malicious or typo-squatted packages.

Worked example. A build needs a library removed from npm yesterday (left-pad style). With a proxy registry cache the build still passes; without it every pipeline fails.

Industry examples. JFrog Artifactory and Sonatype Nexus sit in front of most enterprise builds; in March 2016 the left-pad removal broke thousands of builds worldwide.

Everyday analogy. A warehouse with labelled, sealed boxes you can trace back to the factory batch.

Common interview traps.

  • Overwriting a released version in the registry.
  • Pulling dependencies from the public internet on every build, with no mirror or lockfile.

notes.title: Monorepo pipelines: only run what changed
notes.html:
In a monorepo or multi-service repo, running everything on every change wastes hours. Options: path filters (on.paths: ['services/orders/**']), affected-target detection from a dependency graph (Nx, Bazel, Gradle, Turborepo), and remote caches so unchanged work is reused.

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["services/orders/**", "libs/common/**"]

Caveat: path filters miss dependencies. A change to libs/common must trigger every consumer, so graph-based tools are safer than hand-written filters. Always run the whole suite on a schedule or on main as a safety net.

Industry examples. Google's TAP and Meta's Sapling-based systems only test impacted targets; Nx and Bazel bring the idea to smaller teams.

Everyday analogy. Repainting only the rooms that had leaks, but checking the whole house once a month.

Common interview traps.

  • Required status checks that never run because path filtering skipped them (the PR cannot merge). Use a final "gate" job that always reports.
  • Forgetting shared-library changes.

notes.title: Mobile and Android CI example
notes.html:
An Android pipeline shows how the generic stages look in practice: ./gradlew lint testDebugUnitTest on every PR; instrumented UI tests on an emulator or a device farm (Firebase Test Lab) post-merge; a release build ./gradlew bundleRelease signed with a key from the secrets store; upload the AAB to Play internal track with Fastlane or the Gradle Play Publisher; then staged rollout in the store.

- run: ./gradlew lint testDebugUnitTest
- run: ./gradlew bundleRelease
  env:
    KEYSTORE_B64: ${{ secrets.KEYSTORE_B64 }}   # decoded to a file only in this step
- run: bundle exec fastlane supply --track internal

Gradle build caching and the configuration cache cut times a lot; emulators are slow and flaky, so keep the instrumented suite small and shard it.

Industry examples. Many apps use Bitrise, GitHub Actions or CircleCI mobile images; Google's Play Console supports staged rollouts and halting a rollout.

Everyday analogy. A printing press: proof-read quickly (unit tests), do a test print (internal track), then distribute gradually.

Common interview traps.

  • Keystore committed to the repo.
  • Running every UI test on every PR; keep that suite for post-merge or nightly.

notes.title: Notifications, status checks and pipeline health
notes.html:
The pipeline itself needs observability. Status checks appear on the PR and gate merging. Notify the right people (the author on failure, the team channel for main-branch breaks), avoid spam, and link to logs. Track pipeline metrics: success rate, duration (p50/p95), queue time, flaky-test rate, cost per run.

Rule: a broken main is everyone's top priority. Revert first, fix after; do not stack commits on a red build.

Worked example. p95 pipeline time creeping from 9 to 17 minutes over a quarter is noticed only because a dashboard graphs it; the cause was a new dependency download uncached.

Industry examples. Teams at GitHub and Atlassian publish "build health" dashboards; Slack/Teams bots post failing builds with the culprit commit.

Everyday analogy. A factory's andon cord: anyone can stop the line, and a stopped line is fixed before more product is made.

Common interview traps.

  • Notifications to a channel nobody reads.
  • No ownership of the pipeline itself, so it decays.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: A pipeline is automated, versioned stages ordered fail-fast: lint and unit tests first, slow integration later. In GitHub Actions you write workflows with triggers, jobs, steps and needs; Jenkins and GitLab CI express the same ideas with different syntax and hosting. Keep it fast with dependency caching, parallel jobs and test sharding, and pass artifacts between jobs. Treat the pipeline as a production system: encrypted secrets or OIDC short-lived credentials, least-privilege tokens, pinned actions, approvals before production.

questions.promptHtml: What are the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline and why does their order matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you know "fail fast" and can reason about feedback time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Checkout, restore cache, build, unit test, lint and static analysis, security scan, package into an artifact or image, publish, deploy, then smoke test. Cheap and fast checks go first so a bad change fails in a minute, not after a 30-minute test suite.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Independent checks (lint, unit tests, security scan) can run in parallel. Slow integration and end-to-end tests come later, or after merge. Developers tolerate roughly 10 minutes of waiting; longer pipelines cause context switching and stacked branches.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Slowest stage first.
  • Treating the pipeline as an untracked script instead of reviewed code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you cut a 40-minute pipeline? → Cache dependencies, parallelise and shard tests, run only affected tests, move slow tests post-merge.
  2. What is an artifact? → The output of a stage (jar, image, report) stored for later stages.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior reasons about feedback time and test impact analysis.

questions.promptHtml: Explain workflows, jobs, steps and runners in GitHub Actions. How do you make one job wait for another?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hands-on knowledge of the most common CI syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows triggered by events. It contains jobs, which run in parallel on runners (machines). A job has steps that run shell commands or reusable actions. To order jobs you use needs:, for example deploy needs: test.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Other useful features: strategy.matrix runs a job across values (OS, language versions); concurrency cancels superseded runs; permissions limits the GITHUB_TOKEN; if: conditions restrict jobs to main; environment: adds approvals and environment secrets.

jobs:
  test: { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ {uses: actions/checkout@v4}, {run: npm ci}, {run: npm test} ] }
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ {run: ./deploy.sh} ]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Pinning third-party actions to a movable tag instead of a commit SHA.
  • Default write permissions on GITHUB_TOKEN.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reuse a pipeline across 100 repos? → Reusable workflows or composite actions.
  2. What are self-hosted runners for? → Private network access, special hardware, cost control; they need hardening.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions least-privilege tokens, SHA pinning and concurrency control.

questions.promptHtml: How do Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions differ, and what stays the same?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many companies still run Jenkins; you must translate ideas between tools.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The concepts are identical: a config file in the repo, jobs run on agents or runners, stages, artifacts, caches, secrets. Differences are syntax and operations. Jenkins uses a Groovy Jenkinsfile and you host, patch and scale it yourself, with a big plugin ecosystem. GitLab CI uses .gitlab-ci.yml built into GitLab. Actions uses YAML in .github/workflows and is built into GitHub.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Jenkins' flexibility is also its cost: plugin conflicts, controller upgrades, agent management, security patches. SaaS tools trade control for less maintenance. Reuse: Jenkins shared libraries, GitLab include:, GitHub reusable workflows.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "CI" with Jenkins.
  • Credentials hardcoded in Jenkinsfiles.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Migrating off Jenkins? → Inventory jobs, migrate by value, run both in parallel, retire gradually.
  2. Where do Jenkins builds run? → On agents; the controller should not build.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior discusses total cost of ownership, not just features.

questions.promptHtml: How would you speed up a slow CI pipeline? Explain caching keys.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A practical senior skill with measurable wins.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cache dependency downloads keyed by a hash of the lockfile so the cache is reused until dependencies change, run independent jobs in parallel, shard big test suites across runners, pass build outputs as artifacts instead of rebuilding, and use Docker layer caching.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A good key is something like os-gradle-${hash(**/*.gradle*, wrapper.properties)} with a restore-key fallback to the latest older cache. A key that never changes serves stale dependencies; a key that changes every run never hits. Remote build caches (Bazel, Gradle) share compiled outputs across developers and CI.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Caching build outputs that include secrets.
  • Optimising the build when the real delay is queueing for runners.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure? → Per-stage timing, then attack the largest.
  2. Risk of caches? → Stale or poisoned cache; clean on lockfile change.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior measures first and optimises the longest stage.

questions.promptHtml: How should a pipeline authenticate to a cloud provider to deploy? Why is OIDC preferred over stored access keys?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: CI is a high-value attack target; this tests supply-chain awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With OIDC the pipeline gets a signed identity token from the CI platform, exchanges it with the cloud for a short-lived role, and uses it for the job. No long-lived key is stored, so there is nothing to leak or rotate, and the role can be scoped to one repo, branch and environment.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Static keys in CI variables are readable by any step, including a malicious dependency's install script. With OIDC, the cloud trusts a claim like repo:acme/api:ref:refs/heads/main, so a fork or other branch cannot assume the role. Also: least-privilege tokens, no secrets for fork PRs, pinned actions, approvals on production environments, masked logs.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using pull_request_target to run untrusted PR code with secrets.
  • Assuming log masking hides transformed secrets (base64).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. A key leaked in git history? → Revoke and rotate first; rewriting history is secondary.
  2. How to limit blast radius? → Separate roles per environment with minimal permissions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs trust conditions on token claims and mentions provenance (SLSA).

questions.contextHtml: Your cloud bill spikes 8x overnight. Instances in an unused region are mining cryptocurrency. CloudTrail shows the actions came from the access key stored in the CI system for the deploy user, which has AdministratorAccess. The last change to the pipeline was a new third-party build step added two days ago.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and how do you prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Deletes the instances and carries on, without revoking the key or finding the entry point.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When did misuse start? What else did that key touch (data, IAM, other regions)? Which pipeline runs had the new step?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable and rotate the key, terminate rogue resources, restrict the account with an SCP, preserve logs for forensics.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The new step exfiltrated env vars; a compromised dependency; a fork PR got secrets; log leakage.
  4. How I'd verify: CloudTrail by key and IP, pipeline run logs, diff of the workflow change, dependency changes.
  5. Root cause: A long-lived, over-privileged key exposed to an unpinned third-party step.
  6. Fix: Replace with OIDC short-lived roles scoped per repo and environment; pin actions to SHAs; reduce IAM to deploy-only.
  7. Prevention: Secret scanning, egress restrictions on runners, billing alerts, review of workflow changes through CODEOWNERS.
  8. Trade-offs: More friction adding new actions; accepted for the risk reduction.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Were customers affected? → Check for data access in CloudTrail and S3 logs; involve security and legal.
  • Can we just rotate the key periodically? → It narrows the window but OIDC removes the stored secret entirely.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found a pipeline log containing a base64-encoded token that bypassed masking, which is why they stopped printing environment variables at all.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cleans up resources only.
  • Hire: revokes, rotates, finds the entry point.
  • Strong hire: OIDC, least privilege, supply-chain controls and detection.

questions.promptHtml: How do you avoid copy-pasting pipelines across 100 repositories?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Platform thinking and change management.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Publish a reusable workflow (GitHub), include: template (GitLab) or shared library (Jenkins) owned by a platform team. Repos call it with a few inputs. Version the template (for example @v3) so a change does not break every repo at once, and roll upgrades out gradually.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: This also standardises security steps, scans and deployment. Pipelines live in the repo (pipeline as code), not in a UI, so they are reviewed and reproducible.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Unversioned shared templates.
  • Configuring pipelines only in the Jenkins UI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do teams customise? → Inputs and a small set of extension hooks.
  2. How do you roll out a breaking change? → New major version, migrate repos with automation, deprecate the old one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior includes versioning and migration tooling.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use self-hosted runners, and what must you do to secure them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Runners execute your code with access to secrets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use them for private network access, GPUs or special hardware, large machines, or lower cost at scale. Secure them by making each job run in a fresh ephemeral container or VM, never running untrusted fork code on persistent runners, giving minimal credentials, and autoscaling so queues stay short.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Persistent runners keep files and tokens between jobs, so one compromised job can poison the next. Kubernetes-based runner controllers create a pod per job. Hosted runners are simpler but cost per minute.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Persistent runners reused by all repos.
  • Optimising build speed when queue time is the problem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you size the pool? → Queue-time metrics and autoscaling.
  2. Fork PRs? → Do not give them secrets or self-hosted runners.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior treats runners as a security boundary.

questions.promptHtml: Why use an internal artifact repository or proxy registry?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reliability and supply-chain control.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It stores your immutable, traceable release artifacts and proxies public registries. Builds keep working when npm or Maven Central is down or a package disappears, and you can block malicious or typosquatted packages and enforce retention and scanning.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Release and snapshot repositories are separated; released versions are never overwritten. Artifacts carry commit SHA, build number and SBOM. The 2016 left-pad removal broke thousands of builds that had no mirror.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Overwriting a released version.
  • Fetching from the public internet on every build with no lockfile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is dependency confusion? → A public package overriding an internal name; use scoped names and registry rules.
  2. Retention? → Keep releases, expire snapshots.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links it to supply-chain security and provenance.

questions.promptHtml: Describe a CI/CD pipeline for an Android app.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests applying generic ideas to a real stack.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On each PR run lint and unit tests with Gradle. After merge run instrumented tests on an emulator or device farm. For release build a signed AAB with the keystore from a secrets store, upload to the Play internal track (Fastlane or Gradle Play Publisher), then staged rollout, watching crash-free sessions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Use Gradle build cache and configuration cache. Keep the instrumented suite small and sharded because emulators are slow and flaky. Decode the keystore only in the signing step and never commit it.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keystore in the repo.
  • Running the full UI suite on every PR.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you version builds? → versionCode from the CI build number; versionName from the tag.
  2. How do you halt a bad rollout? → Play Console halt plus a remote-config kill switch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions signing key custody and rollout health gates.

questions.promptHtml: A PR in a monorepo cannot merge because a required check never ran due to path filters. Why, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A real gotcha with required checks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A workflow skipped by path filters never reports a status, so branch protection waits for a check that never appears. Fix by having an always-running gate job that decides what to run and reports success when nothing needed to run, and make that gate the required check.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Path filters also miss shared-library dependencies; graph-based affected detection (Nx, Bazel) is safer. A scheduled full run on main catches anything the filters missed.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hand-written filters that omit shared libs.
  • Making a path-filtered job a required check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternative? → Always run lightweight checks and skip only expensive jobs internally.
  2. How do you validate the filters? → Nightly full runs and compare.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior designs the gate-job pattern and the safety net.

questions.contextHtml: main has been red for 3 days. Eleven PRs have merged on top of the broken build, each author assuming "someone else will fix it". The failing test is in a module owned by a team on leave. Release is scheduled for Friday.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do and what changes afterwards?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Disables the failing test and moves on without finding the cause or setting a rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which commit first turned it red? Is the failure real or flaky? Who owns the module?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find the first bad commit (bisect from CI history) and revert it; freeze merges until green.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A real regression; an environment change; a flaky test masked by "just re-run".
  4. How I'd verify: CI history per commit, re-run on a clean runner, git bisect.
  5. Root cause: No rule or ownership for a red main, and merges were allowed while red.
  6. Fix: Revert, restore green, then fix forward properly.
  7. Prevention: Merge queue so main cannot go red, auto-notify the commit author, a "red main is top priority" rule, pipeline-health dashboard.
  8. Trade-offs: Reverting loses work temporarily, but it is cheaper than stacking changes on a broken base.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Test owner unavailable → the team that merged the breaking change fixes it; ownership is by change, not just by module.
  • Release deadline → release from the last green commit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After adding a merge queue the team never had a red main longer than a few minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables the test.
  • Hire: bisects, reverts, communicates.
  • Strong hire: merge queue, ownership rules and metrics.
